extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP counsel, and patent prosecutors
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate whether asserted patent claims are directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under Alice (35 U.S.C. §101), focusing on whether claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea/natural phenomenon and whether they contain an inventive concept that transforms the claim into patent-eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (e.g., 'using keywords to search hierarchically-arranged data,' 'exchanging information for the purpose of identification,' 'recommending a product based on geographic location and preferences,' 'advancing funds based on future retirement payments,' 'allocating commissions,' etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is characterized as directed to an abstract idea, courts proceed to Alice step two. Examples across cases: claims described as the abstract idea of tailoring webpages based on user data, data distribution, inventory validation, managing trading risk, processing loan applications, and conventional auctions. Multiple holdings treat business practices, fundamental economic concepts, and certain data-manipulation schemes as abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims lack an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claims contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter — i.e., a meaningful limitation beyond the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts repeatedly hold claims ineligible where there is 'no inventive concept' or 'no meaningful limitation' to the abstract idea. Typical determinations find no inventive concept where the claim merely applies the abstract idea using existing or generic technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of generic computer components is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the inclusion of a computer system, generic hardware, or well-known and conventional technology supplies an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across many decisions, 'recitation of a computer system and generic computer equipment' or 'generic computer components' does not supply an inventive concept. Cases hold that merely implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer or using generic devices is insufficient to make claims patent eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to natural phenomena / laws of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim is directed to a natural phenomenon or a law of nature (e.g., 'using T cells to activate the immune system,' correlations between biomarkers and disease, interactions between man-made receptors and bodily fluids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to natural phenomena or laws of nature are ineligible absent additional inventive concept. Courts note that it may be 'plausible' that an invention is patent-eligible if it does not simply isolate or identify a material found in nature, and factual inquiry may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether claimed elements are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional' is a question of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of whether elements recited in the claims are well-understood, routine, and conventional often presents a factual dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts frequently find that whether claim elements are routine and conventional is a question for fact (with competing expert testimony) and therefore summary judgment or dismissal on §101 is inappropriate where genuine disputes exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction may be necessary before deciding eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claim construction has occurred and whether construing claim terms is required to resolve the §101 inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple holdings deny motions to dismiss or for judgment on the pleadings because claim construction had not yet occurred and is necessary to determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea or possess an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prematurity when factual discovery or expert evidence is ongoing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the court should defer ruling on eligibility because factual discovery is incomplete or expert testimony/evidence is needed to evaluate novelty, conventionality, or the asserted inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts deny motions as premature when factual discovery remains ongoing, when plaintiffs have relied on undisclosed expert opinions, or when the availability of evidence (e.g., state of the art, prior uses) is necessary to determine eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered combination of conventional elements can supply an inventive concept if unconventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the ordered combination of elements amounts to an unconventional technological solution rather than merely combining conventional elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some decisions recognize that an 'ordered combination of elements' could be inventive if it uses conventional technology in unconventional ways to solve a problem in the computer field. Courts examine whether the specification suggests that the combination provides an unconventional technological solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-level data/software recitations without detail are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claims that recite high-level software/data processing (e.g., 'taking in and outputting data' with no detail on how data is manipulated) provide patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere recitation of software at a highly abstract level—input, output, and generic manipulation—with no detail on how data is transformed typically fails to provide an inventive concept. Courts have struck down claims that provide no detail as to how data is manipulated between input and output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices and longstanding commercial methods are abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed subject matter embodies fundamental economic practices or long-prevalent commercial methods (e.g., auctions, payment processing, third-party intermediaries, financing applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts repeatedly treat fundamental economic practices as abstract ideas. Claims covering such practices typically require an additional inventive concept to be patent eligible; absent that, they are held ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding conventional testing/collection steps does not add meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether adding routine steps—such as testing prices, collecting data based on customer reactions, or validating inventory by known methods—adds any meaningful limitation to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions hold that the addition of routine or data-collection steps does not convert an abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention because these steps do not provide a meaningful technological limitation beyond the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specialized database/analytics or unconventional technological detail can preserve eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim recites specialized databases, powerful data analytics, or other specific technological implementations that constitute an unconventional solution beyond generic components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some holdings indicate claims should not be dismissed when the complaint alleges 'unconventional technological solution through a specialized database permitting powerful data analytics' or when the specification expressly recites unconventional technical features—these factual allegations may preclude dismissal at early stages.
